proposal.root_problem: The support ticket backlog about refunds is caused by refund submissions being rejected outright at the payment step due to invalid IBAN format (E-01: all 5 sampled failed refunds show status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT), which pushes affected customers to open tickets asking about undelivered refunds — not by slow agent responses, since median agent response time is 2.0h against a 24h SLA across 900 tickets (E-02).
proposal.requested_solution: Build a customer-facing chatbot so customers get instant answers about refund status instead of waiting (initial request from SH-SUP, CL-01).
symptoms: Stakeholder reports customers waiting for refund answers and requests a chatbot (CL-01, CL-02).
A support ticket backlog exists despite agents responding at a median of 2.0 hours, well within the 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets (E-02).
All 5 sampled refund attempts in payment-db failed outright with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01).
causal_chain: A customer submits a refund request with an invalid/incompatible IBAN format.
The payment system rejects the refund at validation, recording status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01).
Because the refund did not complete, the customer does not receive their money and opens a support ticket to ask what happened.
Tickets referencing undelivered refunds accumulate into the reported backlog, even though agents reply within the 24-hour SLA (E-02), so the backlog reflects refund failures, not slow replies.

assumptions.statement: The 5 sampled FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds reflect an ongoing failure pattern rather than a one-off anomaly in a small batch.
Customers whose refunds fail with FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT are a meaningful contributor to the 900-ticket backlog, linking the refund-failure mechanism to the reported 'customers waiting' symptom.

proposal.summary: The support team's initial request (SH-SUP, CL-01) was to build a chatbot because customers were allegedly waiting too long for answers about refunds. Evidence contradicted this: ticket-db shows a 2.0-hour median agent response time against a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets (E-02), while payment-db shows all 5 sampled refund records failed outright with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01). This evidence rejected the 'slow response' and 'capacity' hypotheses and supported H-IBAN-FORMAT-FAILURE, redefining the root problem (PD-1) as refunds being rejected at submission due to invalid IBAN format, which pushes customers to open tickets - not slow agent answering. The DEFINE gate returned CONDITIONAL_PASS, deferring two critical unknowns (ticket-failure correlation share, and data completeness of DA-PAY/DA-TCK) to open verification obligations rather than resolving them. The release decision is RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION with no holds: the only scope actually released is preparing the list of FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT-affected customers for notification (notify_affected_customers:DA-TCK), which is already done. The two full remedies - fixing IBAN validation at submission and proactively contacting affected customers - were judged not feasible within contest time, and no tool exists in the available (read-only) tool surface to deploy such a fix or send outbound notifications. Correlation and data-completeness questions remain open but fall outside the released scope, which is why release proceeded despite them. The release is therefore a partial, limited step (customer-list preparation) toward the real fix, explicitly documented with the open unknowns and infeasible remedies as known limitations.
key_points: Initial request (CL-01, stakeholder SH-SUP) asked for a chatbot to fix slow agent responses to refund queries, but E-02 (ticket-db response_times, 900 tickets) shows a 2.0h median response against a 24h SLA, contradicting that framing; H-SLOW-RESPONSE and H-CAPACITY-UNDERSTAFFING were REJECTED on this basis.

E-01 (payment-db refund_failures, 5 sampled records R-0..R-4) shows all sampled refunds failed with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, supporting H-IBAN-FORMAT-FAILURE: tickets are driven by outright refund rejection at submission, not slow replies. This became the redefined root problem (PD-1).

The DEFINE gate returned CONDITIONAL_PASS: two critical unknowns were deferred rather than resolved - U-TICKET-FAILURE-CORRELATION (what share of the 900-ticket backlog is actually tied to FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT) and U-DATA-COMPLETENESS (whether DA-PAY/DA-TCK completeness supports generalizing the 5-sample finding) - tracked as VOB-U-TICKET-FAILURE-CORRELATION and VOB-U-DATA-COMPLETENESS, both still OPEN.

The final decision is RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION with no holds. What was actually released is the minimum useful scope: notify_affected_customers:DA-TCK (work item W-WI-NOTIFY-PREP, status DONE), i.e. compiling the list of FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refund records to prepare customer outreach.

Broader fixes were explicitly left unfinished: real-time IBAN validation at submission (SR-RM-IBAN-VALIDATION) and proactive customer notification/outreach (SR-RM-NOTIFY-FAILED-REFUNDS) are both marked feasible_in_contest_time=false, and the two correlation/quantification work items are blocked by the open VOBs.

The release decision frames the two open VOBs as outside the committed release scope (their blocking_scope items - correlation, quantification, the validation fix - are not in release_scope), which is why the release could proceed despite those unknowns remaining open.

The tool surface available (ticket-db, payment-db) is read-only, so no tool exists to actually deploy the IBAN validation fix or to send outbound notifications to affected customers; this is recorded as a limitation rather than resolved.
limitations_explained: DEFINE Gate was only a CONDITIONAL_PASS: the gate passed with deferred items, meaning known critical questions were acknowledged but not answered before release.

VOB-U-TICKET-FAILURE-CORRELATION is OPEN and CRITICAL impact - it is unknown what share of the 900-ticket backlog is truly caused by FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds versus other reasons; this blocks correlate_tickets_with_failed_refunds and fix_iban_validation_at_submission, but those items sit outside the released scope.

VOB-U-DATA-COMPLETENESS is OPEN and HIGH impact - DA-TCK completeness is UNKNOWN (DA-PAY is COMPLETE), so it is not confirmed that the 5 sampled failures and the 900-ticket SLA figure represent the full population rather than a partial extract; this blocks quantify_iban_failure_rate.
The 5-sample FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT pattern (assumption A-IBAN-FAILURES-REPRESENTATIVE) is unverified as representative of the full backlog - it is treated as an assumption, not a confirmed fact.

The actual root-cause fix (real-time IBAN validation at submission) and the direct customer-outreach remedy were not implemented in this release: both are marked not feasible in contest time, and no write/deploy or outbound-notification tool exists in the available read-only tool surface (ticket-db, payment-db).
Because DA-TCK completeness is unknown, even the reclassification of the problem (from 'slow response' to 'IBAN format failure') rests on potentially partial underlying data.

A separate, unresolved question (U-VISIBILITY-GAP-CONTRIBUTION, OPEN, not deferred to a VOB) asks whether lack of refund-status visibility independently drives ticket creation beyond IBAN-failure cases; this was not addressed by the released scope.
